# Phoenix View TTL using Phoenix Compactions (WIP)

## **Phoenix TTL for View and Tables**

With Phoenix TTL for views and tables,  the basic gist was the TTL should be a Phoenix view level setting instead of being at the table level as implemented in HBase. More details on the design here ([Phoenix TTL](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1aZWhJQCARBVt9VIXNgINCB8O0fk2GucxXeu7472SVL8/edit#)). Both HBase TTL and Phoenix TTL rely on apply expiration logic during the scanning phase when serving query results and apply deletion logic when pruning the rows from store. In HBase the pruning is achieved during the compaction phase. The initial design and implementation of Phoenix TTL for views used the MR framework to run delete jobs to prune away the expired rows. We knew this was a sub optimal solution since it required managing and monitoring MR jobs. It would also have introduced additional delete markers which would have temporarily added more rows (delete markers) have made the scans less performant. Using the HBase compaction framework instead to prune away the expired rows would fit nicely into the existing architecture and would be efficient like pruning the HBase TTL rows. 

[PHOENIX-6888](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-6888) introduced Phoenix TTL (row-level TTL vs cell level TTL) for tables and Phoenix Compactions. (Design doc [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bVsrdXYAjBcXShb8bN1kvDXyAqCDCyyYkIQXUFfcjQI/edit#heading=h.fcyowuwsyd))

## **Phoenix Data Model**

![][image1]

As can be seen from above the data model consists of the following entities

1. Non Partitioned tables and indexes

2. Partitioned tables.  
   1. Global Views.  
   2. Tenant Views.  
3. Shared indexes.  
   1. Global View Indexes  
   2. Tenant View Indexes  
   3. Local Indexes

In addition the above entities can be

1. Multi-Tenanted  
2. Non Multi-Tenanted  
3. Salted  
   

The TTL matching algorithm needs to handle the above cases.

## **Phoenix View hierarchy specification**

Phoenix views specification allows a HBase table to be further partitioned into virtual tables or updatable views and read-only views. 

The basic gist being a view can be created by selecting all the columns from the base table/view and specifying the where clause which selects the rows that belong to this view.  
More information on views [here](https://phoenix.apache.org/views.html).

[PHOENIX-4555](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-4555) proposes a stricter specification for updateable views but needs to be enforced.  
[PHOENIX-4555](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-4555) should be improved to add the constraint that PK’s should be used in the order they are defined.  
The view specification uses only the where clause to define the view’s data set.  
The view specifications can be used to create perfectly disjointed views on one hand and on the other hand can create all kinds of arbitrary data sets. For example \- Overlapping views (complex where clauses which create non-disjoint data sets)

### **Phoenix View specification example when PHOENIX-4555 is enforced**

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS TEST.PRODUCT (  
   PRODUCT\_ID CHAR(15) NOT NULL,  
   COUNTRY CHAR(2) NOT NULL,  
   SITE VARCHAR NOT NULL,  
   SYSTEM\_MODSTAMP DATE  
   CONSTRAINT PK PRIMARY KEY (  
       PRODUCT\_ID,  
       COUNTRY,  
       SITE  
   )  
) VERSIONS=1, MULTI\_TENANT=true

CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS TEST.US\_ORDERS(  
   ORDER\_ID CHAR(15) NOT NULL,  
   STATE CHAR(2) NOT NULL,  
   DATE DATE NOT NULL,  
   DETAILS VARCHAR,  
   CONSTRAINT PK PRIMARY KEY (  
       ORDER\_ID,  
       STATE,  
       DATE ))   
AS SELECT \* FROM TEST.PRODUCT WHERE COUNTRY \= 'US'  
CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS TEST.UK\_ORDERS(  
   ORDER\_ID CHAR(10) NOT NULL,  
   COUNTY CHAR(3) NOT NULL,  
   DATE DATE NOT NULL,  
   DETAILS VARCHAR,  
   CONSTRAINT PK PRIMARY KEY (  
       ORDER\_ID,  
       COUNTY,  
       DATE ))   
AS SELECT \* FROM TEST.PRODUCT WHERE COUNTRY \= 'UK'

The above views are created in accordance with the constraints specified in PHOENIX-4555.

* View specification (view statements) use only the PK columns  
  * Since table is MULTI\_TENANT \- PRODUCT\_ID is automatically included in the PK list  
  * Can use PKs (COUNTRY, SITE) if needed  
* Sibling view specification uses the same set of PK column(s)  
  * Both views use the same PK (COUNTRY)  
* Sibling and child views use PK columns in the order they are defined. (**PHOENIX-4555 enhancement**)  
  * Both views use the PKs (PRODUCT\_ID, COUNTRY) in the order they were defined

    

**PHOENIX-4555 ensures** 

* **views are disjoint and non-overlapping**   
* **HBase row keys can be efficiently mapped back to the view that created it.**

## 

### **Phoenix View-Index specification and constraints**

* In addition to PHOENIX-4555 constraints, View and Views indexes are further constrained by PHOENIX-7067 specifications  
  * View should be allowed to extend the parent PK i.e. adding its own PK column in the view definition only when there are no indexes in the parent hierarchy  
  * OR in other words \- View indexes can be defined on a given view only when there are no child views that have extended the PK of the base view.

**PHOENIX-7067 ensures that** 

* **index rows get generated AND/OR do not get clobbered when index are defined on views.**

As we can see from the [documentation](https://phoenix.apache.org/views.html) AND [PHOENIX-4555](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-4555), it can lead to 2 types of views.

1. Updatable views (simple where clauses which create disjointed data sets)  
   1. The view statement in updatable view conform to the PHOENIX-4555 specification  
   2. The view statement can only contain AND expressions  
   3. Each expression used in the WHERE clause must use the EQUALS (=) operator  
   4. For e.g CREATE VIEW (...) AS SELECT \* FROM CUSTOM\_ENTITY.CUSTOM\_ENTITY\_DATA\_NO\_ID WHERE KEY\_PREFIX \= 'z00' AND PK1 \= 'pk1'  
        
2. Read-only views (complex where clauses, hence no DMLs allowed)  
   1. The view statement containing expressions other than ANDs (for e.g OR’s, LIKE …)  
   2. The view statement containing operators other than EQUALS. (for e.g \<, \> ..)  
   3. For e.g CREATE VIEW (...) AS SELECT \* FROM CUSTOM\_ENTITY.CUSTOM\_ENTITY\_DATA\_NO\_ID WHERE KEY\_PREFIX \= 'z00' AND PK1 \> 'pk1'

## **Redesign Phoenix TTL for Views using [PHOENIX-6888](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-6888) and [PHOENIX-4555](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-4555)**

### **Assumptions and Constraints:**

* PHOENIX TTL and HBase table-level TTL are mutually exclusive features.  
  * The TTL table property will be used to define a TTL value for Phoenix tables and views when phoenix.table.ttl.enabled=true.  
* Views are created in accordance with PHOENIX-4555 specifications constraints.  
  * View specification (view statements) use only the PK columns  
  * Sibling view specification uses the same set of PK column(s)  
  * Sibling and child views use PK columns in the order they are defined. (**PHOENIX-4555 enhancement**)  
* TTL can be set only on Updatable views  
* There can be only one TTL definition in the hierarchy of tables and views.  
* Each row in the HBase tables belongs to only one view.  
  * Data created by the updatable views are stored in the underlying HBase tables in well partitioned virtual tables. 

### **High Level Requirements:**

* TTL for Phoenix tables/views be expressed in a declarative fashion. (Provided as part of Table/View DDL statements)  
  * Global tables. (different from HBase table level TTL)  
  * For both mutable and immutable views  
  * Global and Tenant Views  
* TTL for Phoenix tables/views can be changed via an ALTER COMMAND and the change should be effective immediately.  
* TTL on Phoenix tables/views specifies the duration since the last modified timestamp of the row when the row expires.  
  * last modified timestamp of the row is defined as the timestamp of the latest empty column for the row.  
* Expired (i.e., dead) rows should not be visible to scans.  
* Partial updates to rows should be possible and still maintain row consistency.  
  * It is possible in partial updates to a row, that certain columns would not be updated for periods greater than TTL duration. Such columns are still considered live and should be included in the scan results.  
* Table/View Indexes inherit the TTL attribute from their base table/views.  
* Child views cannot override the global/base TTL attribute.  
  * Child views will always inherit/use the base view’s TTL attribute value if one is defined.

#### 

### **Syntax for Create Table/View with TTL**

**CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS TEST.UK\_ORDERS** (  
   ORDER\_ID CHAR(10) NOT NULL,  
   COUNTY CHAR(3) NOT NULL,  
   DATE DATE NOT NULL,  
   DETAILS VARCHAR,  
   CONSTRAINT PK PRIMARY KEY (  
       ORDER\_ID,  
       COUNTY,  
       DATE ))   
AS SELECT \* FROM TEST.PRODUCT WHERE COUNTRY \= 'UK' **TTL=60000**

### **Syntax for Alter Table/View with TTL**

**ALTER VIEW IF EXISTS TEST.UK\_ORDERS SET TTL=360000**

## **Design:**

### Having an efficient TTL Metadata Search

During HBase compaction of a table as the compactor visits each row we need to quickly find the TTL to apply for this particular row. For non-partitioned tables (when no views are defined) there is only one TTL defined for the whole table. When views are present/defined on a given table, finding the TTL for the row is not straightforward, since there can be many views defined on a table and each view may have their own TTL defined. We need to first find the view the row belongs to and then visit the view hierarchy to find the TTL that should be applied.

To aid the searching process, it might be useful to store the TTL metadata in a separate column so that it can be efficiently searched, retrieved and cached during the compaction process.

* ### Design Option : Associating a row to a Table/View using row key matching

When a view statement is defined by the constraints articulated in PHOENIX-4555, all rows created by the view can be matched using the where clause of the view statement. The view thus can simply be represented by the single span KeyRange  generated by the expression representing the view statement. This KeyRange will be persisted in the ROW\_KEY\_MATCHER column in SYSTEM.CATALOG for the given view.  
In other words there exists one-to-one mapping between view (defined by tenant, schema, tablename) and ROW\_KEY\_MATCHER KeyRange. Thus associating a given row with a view reduces to matching the row-key of the given HBase row with the ROW\_KEY\_MATCHER column from SYSTEM.CATALOG.

### What is a RowKeyMatcher

* RowKeyMatcher is a byte sequence pattern that can be used to match HBase row keys  
* RowKeyMatcher is the byte sequence formed by concatenating view constants of a given view.  
* RowKeyMatcher is generated when creating a view.  
* RowKeyMatcher byte array is stored in SYSTEM.CATALOG as part of the view header.

![][image5]

### High Level Matching Algorithm

* Given a HBase row key, find the RowKeyMatcher byte sequence that matches from all the given RowKeyMatcher’s for a given table and given region.  
  * Search uses a in-memory Trie index  
  * The Trie index is created to hold the RowKeyMatcher’s for a batch of views based on the region boundaries

### RowKeyMatcher matching algorithm

| Multi- Tenant | Salted | Shared- Index | HBase Row Key Layout | Action |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| true | true | true | **salt | view-index-id | tenant-id | rest-of-key** | **skip the salt-byte and start matching at the view-index-id (pk position 1\)** |
| true | true | false | **salt | tenant-id | rest-of-key** | **skip salt byte \+ tenant-id to search the global space (pk position 2), if global search returned no results then search in tenant space (pk position 1\)** |
| true | false | true | **view-index-id | tenant-id | rest-of-key** | **start matching at the view-index-id (pk position 0\)** |
| true | false | false | **tenant-id | rest-of-key** | **skip tenant-id to search the global space (pk position 1), if global search returned no results then search in tenant space (pk position 0\)** |
| false | true | true | **salt | tenant-id | rest-of-key** | **skip the salt-byte and start matching at the view-index-id (pk position 1\)** |
| false | true | false | **salt | rest-of-key** | **skip salt byte to search the global space (pk position 1\)** |
| false | false | true | **view-index-id | rest-of-key** | **start matching at the view-index-id (pk position 0\)** |
| false | false | false | **key** | **Start at pk position 0 to search the key space.** |

## **TTL and Phoenix compaction in practice**

During Phoenix compaction various configuration settings like KEEP\_DELETED\_CELLS, VERSIONS, TTL determine the output of the pruned/compacted store files. In HBase these are defined at the column family level. Since many of these configurations do not make sense at the view/partition level and/or would make the implementation more complex.   
We will be simplifying the configuration by only allowing the specification of the TTL \- The Phoenix TTL at one level in the hierarchy. KEEP\_DELETED\_CELLS and VERSIONS will not be allowed to be specified during table and view creation.
